children.text: If you feel unhappy about the way you look and focus a lot on your shape and weight, sometimes you might not feel good about yourself. Anyone can have any type of negative body image. For example, you might feel pressure to have more defined muscle bulk or, to be slim or small. This can be affected by the society and culture you’re part of. You might see yourself differently from how other people see you. For example, friends might say nice things about the way you look but you find it very hard to believe. You might find yourself doing things like: checking yourself in the mirror taking photos and selfies of your body measuring yourself comparing yourself against people you consider to be a better shape focussing on a specific part of your body While this can make you feel better for a little while, in the long term it can it usually makes you feel worse. Instead, it can be helpful to focus on other important parts of life like: how you’re getting on with your friends and family how your work or hobbies are going things you’re planning and looking forward to

Sometimes you might avoid looking at yourself because it leads to intense negative feelings. This can include avoiding: mirrors your reflection in windows getting undressed having baths and showers exercise – as you’re worried about getting changed and others seeing your body You might also wear baggy clothes to hide your body. The problem with avoidance is that you don’t get the opportunity to prove yourself wrong. Instead, it can be helpful to challenge the thoughts you have about yourself.

Rather than avoiding your reflection in the mirror you could look at yourself and describe 2 things you like about yourself. You may say ‘I like the colour of my hair and I like my hands.’ If this is too hard you could ask yourself what 2 positive things your best friend would say about your reflection. It can be helpful to focus on all the things your body does rather than your worries about it. For example, you could say things like: ‘I’m grateful that I’m able to run and keep up with my children’ ‘I’m really glad I can smell my favourite perfume’ ‘I’m happy my body allows me to express myself by wearing my favourite clothes’ ‘I’m really glad that I can play the guitar and sing with my friends’ In this video, psychologist Dr Lynne Taylor shares advice for parents to help teens feel more positive about themselves. Although this video mentions parents and teens, the advice can help anyone who is worried about body image. Listen to the Young Scot podcast about being confident in your body.

SilverCloud is a website with online courses you can do to improve your mental wellbeing. It’s designed by clinical experts, and supported by the NHS and Scottish Government. SilverCloud is free, and you’ll need an email address to sign up. Sign up for SilverCloud’s space for positive body image This is a practical online course that will help you to build a positive body image.
When you go into the SilverCloud site for the first time, enter the access code ‘NHS24’.

Having good, strong supportive relationships makes it easier to manage the day-to-day challenges of life. You’re likely to have people you spend time with that make you feel positive about life and yourself, including your body. There may also be people in your family who focus on weight and shape. This could be a granny who comments negatively on how someone looks. Or someone at work who talks about what they shouldn’t be eating, or their insecurities about their body. It’s important to notice this and think about how these people leave you feeling. It can also be helpful to reflect on which people make you feel positive about yourself and life. Some things to consider are: Can you spend more time with them and less with the people who make you feel bad? In your family, if there are people who constantly bring up your shape or weight is there someone else in your family who can help you challenge this? Can you or someone else help steer the conversation in a different direction?

You might be part of a club, social or community group. It can depend on the environment and culture of these groups whether they’re helpful to you or make you feel worse. For example, some gyms and running clubs are very body focussed, while others may be focussed on what your body can do. It may be helpful to think about what people talk about in the group. You may need to try a few different places to find the right one. Any community group or hobby can have people or places that lead to unhelpful conversations and thoughts. It’s important to be aware of this and not be afraid to stop doing something that’s making you feel bad. Try to find something you enjoy with people you want to be around.

Social media can be a really helpful resource, however one risk is that it can focus attention on unrealistic body ideals. Some platforms lend themselves to passive scrolling of images and this can create a sense of dissatisfaction with your own body. Try to notice which content makes you laugh and feel better and which leaves you feeling more self critical. You could try to: add people who make you laugh add images of landscapes or animals that make you smile try to reduce the amount of information about weight, shape and diet coming onto your phone or device delete unhelpful apps from your phone YoungScot have a podcast on body image, social media and fashion

Online communities can be a good way to stay in touch with friends and family and join groups that interest you. However, some people online can talk negatively about their bodies in a way that may be unhelpful to you. This can be friends, influencers or other people in the communities you’re in. Tailor your online experience to people who make you feel confident and positive about yourself. If you don’t want to remove someone online, you could temporarily mute them.

There’s a free, Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) based, self esteem self-help guide on NHS inform which aims to help you: learn more about self-esteem understand the effects of low self-esteem find ways of improving your self-esteem

children.text: There are many different breathing and relaxation exercises. These focus on slowing your breathing and aim to take your mind off uncomfortable thoughts or symptoms. This can help you relax and make you feel calmer. Breathing exercises can also help: stress anxiety panic anger sleep
Practice different breathing and relaxation exercises until you find one that works for you.

Over time, breathing and relaxation exercises may become something you do automatically if you’re tense or stressed. This can help you become more relaxed. You’ll get the most benefit if you do breathing exercises regularly as part of your daily routine. Find out more about doing breathing exercises

symptoms_seed.name: Tips for doing breathing and relaxation exercises

children.text: Breathing exercises only take a few minutes. You can do them anywhere, including: standing up sitting in a chair that supports your back lying on a bed lying on a yoga mat on the floor

It can take time and practice to feel the benefit of doing these exercises, so it’s important to do them regularly. You should try to set aside 30 minutes, 2 or 3 times each day to practice breathing and relaxation exercises. The more you practice, the better you’ll get and the more effective they’ll be. The differences can feel very small at first, but as time goes on you’ll notice an improvement in your mood and ability to stay calm in stressful situations.

Once you can do relaxation exercises, you can use them whenever, and wherever, you need to throughout the day. To do this you can use a ‘cue’. This is something that’ll catch your eye and remind you to: drop your shoulders check your breathing relax the muscles in your body An example of a ‘cue’ could be a small coloured dot on your watch, or a room in your home. This will act as your reminder.

The Steps for Stress breathing and relaxation playlist is an audio guide. It aims to help you control stress and understand where it comes from. The first 2 tracks will help you understand more about how and why breathing exercises work. You can download this playlist to listen to it anywhere. The audio is also available in BSL.
British Sign Language (BSL)

Before you begin practicing a breathing exercise, it might help to: Find a place where you won’t be disturbed. Make yourself as comfortable as possible. Loosen any clothes that restrict your breathing and take off your shoes, if you like. If you’re lying down, place your arms a little bit away from your body with your palms up. Straighten you legs or bend your knees so your feet are flat on the floor. If you’re sitting, place your arms on the chair arms and put both feet flat on the ground. Put your feet roughly hip-width apart. When you first start practicing these exercises, try to do them when you’re feeling calm. This means you’ll be able to focus on and learn the techniques. If you’re already angry or upset, try using the controlled breathing exercise first. Don’t worry if you can’t relax immediately. Thoughts might pop into your mind but don’t focus on them. Just let them pass through. You could make a note of how relaxed you were before and after the exercises to see if it’s helped.
Don’t rush to get up after relaxation exercises. Sit or lie with your eyes closed for a few minutes to avoid feeling dizzy. Open your eyes and make sure you feel all right before standing up.
The steps to deal with stress leaflet has advice on relaxation and relieving stress. Download the steps to deal with stress leaflet
Stop if you feel any discomfort or pain when doing breathing exercises.

children.text: To practice: Sit in a comfortable chair or lie down. Put one hand on your tummy and one hand on your chest. Close your mouth and take a slow, deep breath in through your nose. Blow the air out slowly and gently through pursed lips. Continue to breathe in through your nose and out through your mouth for 3 to 5 minutes.

You could build up the length of this exercise over time. It can be helpful to count steadily from 1 to 5 as you breathe in, and again when you breathe out. You may not be able to reach 5 at first. When you breathe in, you want your tummy to get bigger. Try to move your tummy but not your chest. Every time you breathe in, let your breath flow as deep down into your belly as is comfortable, without forcing it.

children.text: There are different distraction techniques. In time you may come up with some of your own too. You could: count backwards from 100 in threes – for example, ‘100, 97, 94, 91…’ listen to music count all the red objects you can see repeat the words of a song in your head or out loud do something you enjoy that needs focus – like knitting, sewing, reading or watching a TV show If you can, go outside to sit or walk. Try to focus on the world around you. For example, feel the air on your face and the ground under your feet. Look around at everything that’s going on and listen to all the sounds. Another distraction technique is to picture something or someone that makes you feel happy and relaxed. For example, you could picture your favourite place in your mind, and imagine yourself there with your favourite person, or your pet.
Trishna explains how meditation and relaxation helps her.

children.text: To do the exercise, lie on your back and get comfortable. If you have lower back issues, it can help to put a pillow under your knees. Take a breath in and tense the muscles in one area of your body. Hold the tension for a few seconds. Breathe out and release the tension. Let the muscles relax. Repeat this process in different parts of the body. You can go through this list of body parts: right hand and arm left hand and arm right leg and foot left leg and foot stomach chest back muscles shoulders neck and throat face When you’ve gone through the list, focus on each body part. If you notice any remaining tension, allow it to release as you breathe out.
Progressive muscle relaxation uses your whole body, but if there’s an area of your body that’s painful you can miss it out.

symptoms_seed.name: Common reactions to a traumatic event

children.text: In a stressful or dangerous situation, your body has a survival response. This is often called the fight, flight or freeze response. This means your body is getting ready to tackle the source of the stress, escape or freeze. You won’t choose your response. It’ll happen instinctively.

The fight or flight response will cause your body to go into a state of hyperarousal. This is to get ready for action and focus on the threat. It may feel like: your heart is beating faster you’re breathing more quickly you need to go to the toilet you have pins and needles

Hypo-arousal is when your body freezes in response to a threat. It means your heart and breathing rate will slow down and your blood pressure will drop. You may also feel like things aren’t real, or that you’re watching things from outside your body. This is your body’s way of protecting you when escape isn’t physically possible. Depending if, or how much this happens, you may remember lots or very little about the experience.

There’s no right or wrong way to feel after a challenging or traumatic incident. Anyone involved, whether directly or indirectly, can experience a range of emotions and reactions. You may feel: anxious and afraid – this may be triggered by a reminder of what happened, even when you’re now safe sad, upset or be grieving – especially if you’ve experienced loss cut off and distant from others and the world around you numb, disconnected or that things seem unreal it’s difficult to accept what happened shame or guilt about what you did or didn’t do during and after the incident confusion, guilt or even elation if you survived and others didn’t angry or aggressive irritable You may notice that you: think a lot about what happened find it difficult to concentrate and/or become forgetful are trying to avoid people, places or situations that remind you of what happened are working hard to not think about what happened act recklessly or in self-destructive ways You may experience: vivid memories (including images, sounds or smells) during the day frightening dreams physical symptoms like sweating, a racing heart, shaking, a churning stomach and headaches changes in your appetite and energy problems sleeping You may experience some, none or all of these and that’s OK.

There are some things you can do yourself to help you cope after a traumatic event. Some organisations and different types of technology, including sleep and wellbeing apps, provide support too. Find out more about coping after a traumatic event

children.text: There are some steps you can take to support your recovery after a traumatic event.

Reach out to family, friends, colleagues and other people you trust for support. You may not want to talk, but being amongst others can help you feel supported and connected. You’re also less likely to feel isolated or alone. If you do feel able to talk about what happened, this can help your brain make sense of what you’ve been through. Over time, this can help to reduce distressing thoughts, memories or dreams.

Trauma can disrupt your routine but re-establishing it can help your recovery. Having a routine is predictable so it may bring back feelings of safety and control. It can also help to regulate your nervous system which goes into high alert after a traumatic event. A routine encourages healthy habits around meals, sleep, activity and exercise. This can help you build up your confidence and re-establish connections.

Good quality sleep allows your body and mind to rest and recharge. It’s also important for your physical and mental health. If you’re having trouble with sleep, there are things that will help. For example, try to have a set sleep routine and do things before bed that help you feel calm and relaxed. You could also use the Sleepio app. This is a 6 week programme to treat insomnia. You may find it helpful to work through a sleep problems and insomnia self-help guide. This uses cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and expert advice to help manage sleep problems.

Keeping active helps your physical and mental health. It boosts mood and uses up the stress hormone adrenalin. Try to find an activity that suits you. It could be a social activity, like football, or you may enjoy doing something alone like cycling. Whatever you choose, it’s helpful to try and do it regularly. However, doing activity doesn’t have to be about sport or fitness. Anything that gets you moving counts, including walking the dog or gardening. If you can’t exercise, due to an injury or a change in your circumstances, it’s important to have other things you can do instead. For example, relaxation exercises or socialising with others.

When you’re stressed, your body needs you to eat well, even if you don’t feel like it. This will help give you the energy and nutrients you need. It can be helpful to: maintain or re-establish regular eating habits eat as healthily as you can stay hydrated avoid too much alcohol and caffeine plan out your meals in advance stick to regular mealtimes

Relaxation produces the feel-good hormone serotonin which can improve your mood. There may be activities that help you relax like: reading listening to music cooking walking If you can, practice the activity that helps you feel most relaxed regularly. It’s also good to have some quick techniques that you can use when you feel your stress levels rising. For example, breathing and relaxation exercises can reduce physical tension. This may help you feel less stressed. You might find that breathing and relaxation exercises work immediately. However, sometimes you may have to practice them over time before they start to work. You may also find the Daylight app helpful. This is a digital program designed to help reduce stress and worry.

In the days and weeks after a traumatic experience, your brain will try to make sense of the event and come to terms with the aftermath. This means you may find yourself thinking and dreaming about what happened. Although this can be upsetting, it’s a natural part of your recovery. Try to allow your mind and body to do this, rather than pushing the thoughts and feelings away. Talking to others can help, but so can taking time on your own to reflect on your experience.

It may be helpful to connect with others who have been through the same or a similar experience. You may be able to relate to each other and provide each other with support. Find out more about support for people who have experience a traumatic event

Try to avoid using alcohol or other substances to cope with painful feelings. These may bring relief in the short-term, but they usually cause more problems in the long term. Alcohol or drugs may hide difficult memories and feelings when you’re using them. However, when you stop, the thoughts and feelings will still be there. This prevents your brain from processing the event so the pain and distress will last longer. You could try alternative strategies to help you cope like getting support from people you trust. Find out more about where to get support with alcohol
Some people may try to reduce or block their feelings after a traumatic event. However, these coping methods can cause their own problems.

Try to avoid watching too much TV or accessing too much social media around the event. Whilst some information may be helpful, too much can keep you focused on the trauma and may cause more distress. You need time and space away from constant reminders to begin to turn your body’s alarm system down.

It may feel like it’s helpful to withdraw from others or avoid places or situations that remind you of what happened. However, this can leave you feeling isolated and alone. Your thoughts and feelings may also become harder to manage in the long term.

symptoms_seed.name: Support for people who have experienced a traumatic event

children.text: Breathing Space is a free and confidential phone service for people in the region who may be feeling stressed, anxious or depressed. Phone 0800 83 85 87 (6pm to 2am on weekdays and 24 hours at the weekend). Phone calls are free from landlines and mobiles.
The Childline website has advice on children and their worries about the world.

Cruse the region offers help and support for people dealing with all types of grief. If you’re over 18, you can chat to someone from Cruse the region online. The service is open Monday to Friday, from 9am to 9pm. You can also phone the free helpline on 0808 802 6161. This is open: Monday to Friday, 9am to 8pm weekends, 10am to 2pm They also provide free bereavement support for workplaces affected by suicide.

Lifelines is an NHS project. It helps emergency staff and volunteers stay safe and well in their roles. However, the information and support they offer can help the wider public too. You may find it helpful to look at the Lifelines advice on: Understanding my response to trauma and stress What can I do if I’m not ok?
Ready the region have advice on coping with trauma if you’ve been involved in, or affected by, a major incident. This advice is for both adults and children.
The Royal College of Psychiatrists has information about post-traumatic stress disorder. This includes examples of what can cause it and how it can be treated.
Samaritans are open 24 hours a day, 365 days a year to listen and help you, whatever you’re going through. To get in touch you can: phone Samaritans for free on 116 123 email jo@samaritans.org

Young Scot provides guidance and advice to young people feeling worried or concerned about events happening around the world. You can explore topics like: mental health and emotional wellbeing climate and nature You can also listen to the This is How AyeFeel Podcast which covers topics like climate anxiety and mental health.

You can speak to your primary care physician practice or contact a support organisation if you: have experienced a traumatic event have seen a traumatic event are supporting someone who has experienced a traumatic event Many organisations provide a helpline or online chat. You can use these to speak to a professional about a traumatic event. This may help you come to terms with what you’ve seen. Organisations often have information online where you can also get further advice and support.

If you’ve performed CPR on someone or you have seen someone getting CPR, you may find yourself struggling to process what’s happened. Chest, Heart and Stroke the region (CHSS) have an Advice Line that can help. The Advice Line has trained healthcare professionals who will listen to you. They’ll help you process what you’ve experienced and provide advice and support. Further information on the CHSS Advice Line
Children First’s support line is the region’s free helpline, email and webchat service for anyone caring for or concerned about a child. Phone 08000 28 22 33 free (Monday to Friday, 9am to 9pm).

NHS inform has advice on coping with grief. You can: read an article with advice and support on coping with grief complete a self-help guide on coping with bereavement watch some videos on moving through grief

It’s natural to experience shock if you’re told someone has died suddenly. However, you don’t need to manage alone. It’s helpful to speak to family, friends or a support service. You can do this straight away or in time. Try to talk about the person you have lost and explain how you’re feeling. Your primary care physician is also there to support you. You could make an appointment with your primary care physician if you think it would help.

If you lose someone in traumatic circumstances like suicide, there’s a lot to take in. Processes need to take place involving the Police and Procurator Fiscal. This will delay the usual ways that a death is marked for many days or, in some cases, weeks. This can place extra stress on loved ones who are already grieving. Although many people find support with family and friends, others may need extra help. Speak to your primary care physician if you need support after a traumatic event. They can help refer you to support services. You can also contact certain services directly. This includes: Child Bereavement the region Cruse the region Samaritans
The NSPCC website has information on talking to children about difficult topics.

symptoms_seed.name: What to do after a traumatic event

children.text: Experiencing a traumatic event can cause a range of emotions or reactions. You might have: difficulty sleeping upsetting dreams lots of thoughts about what happened difficulty concentrating or making decisions You might feel: scared sad guilty angry irritable or on edge anxious or worried exhausted low numb These can develop immediately after a traumatic event or in the days and weeks that follow. Sometimes you may not notice any of these feelings or symptoms. Although you’ve been through something difficult and distressing, you may feel fine. Find out more about common reactions to a traumatic event

To help you cope after a traumatic event, it can be helpful to: give yourself time and space to recover spend time with people who care about you and talk to them if you’re able try to keep to a regular routine, where possible allow yourself to think about what’s happened so that your brain has a chance to process the memory accept that this experience will shape you and become part of your life story It can be painful and distressing to think or talk about what happened so it may seem helpful to avoid this. However, although this may feel better in the short term, long term avoidance can get in the way of your recovery. Find out more about coping after a traumatic event

Psychological First Aid (PFA) is a set of flexible and practical guidelines. They’re used to care for and support people after a traumatic event. You don’t need to be a professional to offer PFA. It can be offered by anyone. If you’re supporting someone after they’ve been involved in a difficult or traumatic event, consider the following.

Start with the basics and find out what help you can offer. You could consider practical things like: Do they need medical care? Are they in a safe place? Do they need food, drink or clothing? Have they got somewhere to stay? Do they need help with child care? Is their mobile phone charged? Once you’ve found out what they need, ask if they want your help. If they do, you can then help them develop a plan and support them through it.

Emotional reactions are natural after a traumatic event. It’s important to communicate this to the person you’re supporting. Try to remember it yourself too. If they’re panicky or distressed, try to help them feel more in control of their emotions. You could talk calmly and help them regulate their breathing. This can help bring their attention to the present. If they’re distressed, offer comfort and support. Spend time with them and allow them to explain how they’re feeling, if they feel comfortable with this.

After something frightening or shocking, the body goes througha natural recovery process. In most cases, with time, the body’s alarm system will re-set and the experience will be filed away in memory. Gradually the person will start to come to terms with what’s happened. Helping someone understand this reaction can: empower them give them choice reduce shame and self-blame Find out more about common reactions to a traumatic event
Once you’ve found out what help someone needs, you can offer to support them with this. You could also connect them to an organisation that can offer further support.

Providing information on helpful coping strategies can support a healthy recovery after a traumatic event. Without healthy coping methods, people may rely on other unhealthy and unhelpful strategies. For example, pushing their thoughts or emotions away or using substances to numb themselves.

Good social support is key to recovering from a traumatic event. However, traumatic events can disrupt social support. Talk to people about their social network. Where possible, support them to connect with people they feel safe with. It’s also important to help family and friends understand what’s going on. You could pass on information about common reactions to a traumatic event, or share advice about healthy coping methods. If no one is available at home to provide support, you could help make a plan on where they might find support.

Talking to others can help. Breathing Space is a free and confidential phone service for people in the region who may be feeling stressed, anxious or depressed. Phone 0800 83 85 87 (6pm to 2am on weekdays and 24 hours at the weekend). Phone calls are free from landlines and mobiles. You can also phone {{LOCAL_EMERGENCY_NUMBER}} and choose the mental health option. You’ll then be connected to the Mental Health Hub to speak to one of NHS 24’s Psychological Wellbeing Practitioners (PWPs). You can speak to the occupational health team at your school, university or work. They’ll be able to tell you about resources to support your physical and mental health. They may also be able to provide practical advice, if needed. For example, your rights on taking time off work, financial support and getting emergency childcare. Find out about when to get more help after a traumatic event
Think about whether there’s anything you can do to make them feel physically or emotionally safer. There may be ways to protect them from more trauma or distress too.

children.text: It’s difficult to think clearly when you feel scared or anxious. If you can, take time out to physically calm down. Try and get away from what’s upsetting you. For example, you could do another activity for 15 minutes.
walk around the block make a cup of tea have a bath do a breathing exercise drink a glass of water watch a funny video

If you start to get a faster heartbeat or sweaty palms, try not to fight it. Stay where you are and let yourself feel the fear, even though it will be uncomfortable. Place the palm of your hand on your stomach and breathe slowly and deeply. The aim is to get your mind get used to coping with panic, which takes away the fear of feeling panicky.

The Steps for Stress breathing and relaxation playlist is an audio guide. It aims to help you control stress and understand where it comes from. The first two tracks will help you understand more about how and why breathing exercises work. You should listen to them first so you get the most out of the breathing exercises. You can download this playlist to listen to it anywhere. The audio is also available in BSL.

Avoiding fears only makes them worse. But, gradually exposing yourself to the thing you’re scared of can help you maintain control and overcome your fear. If you face your fear you might find that it isn’t as scary as you thought. For example, if you panic getting into a lift one day, it’s best to get back into a lift the next day. Learn about ways to face your fears

Many people struggle with ‘must’ or ‘should’ thoughts. This means they believe in thoughts like life should be perfect, that they should always be calm and that strong people never struggle. Thinking this way causes more fear and anxiety in the long run. So, remember that life is messy and you don’t have to be critical of yourself all the time.

Take a moment to close your eyes and imagine a place of safety and calm. It could be a picture of: you walking on a beautiful beach you snuggled up in bed with the cat next to you a happy memory from childhood Let the positive feelings soothe you until you feel more relaxed.

Sharing your fears can make them less scary. Try talking to someone about what you’re feeling. You could also call a helpline like: Breathing Space – phone 0800 83 85 87 (available from 6pm Friday to 6am Monday, and 6pm to 2am Monday to Thursday) Samaritans – phone 116 123 (available 24 hours a day)
Living Life offers cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) over the phone. You can phone them on {{LOCAL_EMERGENCY_NUMBER}} (Monday to Friday, 9am to 9pm). Further information on Living Life

Living a healthier lifestyle can be very helpful for your mental wellbeing. If you feel healthier, you may find you feel less afraid and anxious. It’s also a good idea to avoid unhealthy habits. Lots of people turn to alcohol or drugs to try to reduce their anxiety, but these things only make it worse. Learn more about eating well Learn more about keeping active

Finally, give yourself a treat when you achieve something despite being afraid. You could: treat yourself to a massage have a meal out buy a new book or another little gift that makes you happy watch a film
British Sign Language (BSL)

Anxiety and fear can feel overwhelming. You might notice physical symptoms of anxiety and panic like a fast heartbeat or shortness of breath. You might worry that these symptoms could be a sign of a serious health problem. In turn, these worries can increase feelings of anxiety. It’s important to remember that these physical symptoms are a normal response to anxiety. It’s your body’s way of trying to protect you from something that seems like a threat and should pass as the anxiety eases. If you’re concerned about your symptoms or your health, speak to your primary care physician practice.

It can sometimes help to challenge unhelpful thoughts. If you ask yourself the right questions, you can show yourself there isn’t anything to worry about. For example, if you’re scared of getting trapped in a lift, you could ask yourself questions like: “Have you ever heard of someone getting trapped in a lift?” “Does the lift look broken?” “Is there any reason to think that if I did get stuck, help would take a long time to arrive?”

children.text: Being active won’t make stress disappear, but it can help to reduce some of the intense emotions you’re feeling. It can also help to clear your thoughts. This will help you deal with your problems more calmly. There are lots of ways to be more active. Activities with breathing exercises and movement are particularly helpful for stress. One example of this is yoga. Find out more about keeping active

A good support network can be important in dealing with stress. It means you have people to turn to for help. If you’re feeling stressed, talk to colleagues, friends and family. If you would like to meet new people, try a new activity or support group. Talking to others can help you find solutions to your problems by letting you see things in a different way. You could also arrange time to relax with people you’re close to. For example, arrange time for a coffee, or to do an activity you all enjoy. This can be a good distraction and stress reliever.

Make some time for exercise, socialising and relaxation to improve your stress levels. You could set aside a couple of nights a week for ‘me time’. Doing this can make you less likely to work overtime or plan something demanding. Sometimes ‘me time’ can be as simple as having a bath or spending time in your garden or local park.

Look for the positives in life and things that you’re grateful for. This can help to put stress in perspective. For example, you could write down 3 things that went well in your day, or 3 things that you’re grateful for. Get some tips for lifting your mood when you’re feeling stressed

Setting yourself goals and challenges helps to build confidence. This will help you deal with stress. You could set goals at work or outside of work. For example, you could try to learn a new language or take up a new sport. By continuing to learn, you become more emotionally resilient. It gives you knowledge and makes you want to be more active. Find out more about how learning new things can improve your mental wellbeing

Working smarter means prioritising your tasks. You should concentrate on the things you need to do that will make a real difference, and leave less important tasks to last. You may also have to accept that your ‘to do’ list will not be complete by the end of the day. As long as the most important tasks are done well, this is OK. Learn more about managing your time

If you remain passive and think ‘I can’t do anything about my problem’, your stress will get worse. That feeling of loss of control is one of the main causes of stress, and negatively affects your wellbeing. Taking control is empowering. It’s a crucial part of finding a solution. Use a problem-solving self-help guide to tackle one of your challenges

Changing a difficult situation isn’t always possible. Try to concentrate on the things you do have control over. For example, if your company is making redundancies, there’s nothing you can do about it. In a situation like that, you need to focus on the things that you can control. Learn about mindfulness and relaxation techniques that can help with acceptance

Helping other people can help you become more resilient and positive. There are many ways to support others, including through volunteer or community work. If you don’t have time to volunteer, try to do someone a favour every so often. For example, bring a cake to work or support a charity fundraiser.

Don’t rely on alcohol, smoking and caffeine as ways of coping with stress. These habits might provide temporary relief, but they won’t make the problems disappear. It’s better to try to tackle the causes of stress. Try to replace unhealthy habits with healthy ones like: going for walks dancing to music making something healthy to eat when you need a break Start to tackle the causes of your stress

symptoms_seed.name: How to manage stress at work

children.text: If your workload is causing stress, think about how much work you can take on. You may think you have no choice but to overwork. But knowing how to say no can be an important part of managing workplace stress. Try to have the confidence to say ‘no’ when you think it’s the right decision, even if this is not the most popular choice. Outline your reasons for this and offer a solution. For example, you could say you will work on a new task after completing another more urgent task. If you take on too much, you could end up doing nothing well. It’s better to say no to some tasks so that you can complete others better. Before saying yes to work, you could calculate how long you’ll need to deal with your current workload. This means you can see if you have any extra capacity.

Speak to someone you feel comfortable with about how you’re feeling. This could be your manager, or someone else in your organisation. Employers have a duty to ensure the health, safety and welfare of their employees. This comes under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974. Employers must also carry out risk assessments for work-related stress. Your employer may be able to make reasonable adjustments for you at work. This could include allowing you to: work from home, where possible take short, frequent breaks extend deadlines for tasks If the reason you’re stressed isn’t work-related, your workplace may still be able to support you. For example, your manager may be able to reduce your workload while you resolve the stress in your personal life.
HSE supports anyone who handles work-related stress in an organisation. This could be: someone in human resources (HR) a health and safety officer trade union representatives line managers

There are many ways to manage stress, but some people turn to ways of coping that are harmful. For example, smoking or alcohol. It’s important to choose healthy ways to deal with stress. You could try: breathing and relaxation exercises being more active spending time with friends and family Find out more about handling stress

Learn to recognise the physical effects of stress so that you can do something about it early. The main symptoms of stress include: a pounding heart or palpitations a dry mouth headaches odd aches and pains loss of appetite loss of libido (sex drive) Be aware of the risk of work stress spilling over into other areas of your life. For example, stress can affect your family life and friendships, or affect your ability to enjoy your hobbies.

There are ways to get help for stress outside your organisation. You can phone and speak to a Breathing Space adviser on 0800 83 85 87. Breathing Space is open 24 hours at the weekend, from 6pm on Fridays to 6am on Mondays, and from 6pm to 2am on weekdays. You could also contact your primary care physician practice for further help.

symptoms_seed.name: Find the right therapist for you

children.text: Your primary care physician may be able to refer you to a local service for counselling or therapy. This means you may not be able to choose your therapist. You do not have to stick with a counsellor or therapist you’re not happy with. If it’s not working, you can ask to be referred to a different therapist. You may have to wait for another therapist to become available.

If you want to have counselling or therapy privately, check that the therapist is accredited by a professional body. For example, the British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy (BACP). Counselling and Psychotherapy in the region (COSCA) has a list of therapists throughout the region.

If you’re having private counselling or therapy, think about what kind of therapist you want. For example, you could think about whether you’d like your therapist to be: a particular gender someone with the same background as you (or different) someone your age or older Feeling comfortable with your therapist or counsellor is important. It can affect how well your talking therapy goes. You may wish to search for a therapist who specialises in dealing with specific groups. For example, LGBTQIA+, neurodivergence, or people who have experienced trauma.

A good therapist: listens to what you say values what you say shows empathy and understanding doesn’t talk down to you checks you’re getting what you want from therapy deals with any worries you may have about the therapy, like how you’ll manage when it comes to an end

Counselling involves talking to a trained therapist. This can be one-to-one, in a group, or with your partner or family. It allows you to look deeper into your problems and worries, and deal with troublesome habits. Psychological therapies are evidence-based psychological treatments that can help improve your health. They help you make changes to your thinking, behaviour and relationships. They’re used to treat mental health difficulties and improve your physical health. Find out more about counselling and therapies

Talking therapies can mean opening up about your private thoughts and feelings. This means it’s important that the therapist puts you at ease. You should feel able to talk openly without getting too nervous or embarrassed. You can use the first session to find out if this is the right therapist for you. You could ask yourself some questions like: Do I feel comfortable telling this person intimate details about my life? Would I be more comfortable with a different person? Do I like their manner towards me? Do I trust them? Do I feel safe with them? Do I feel they want what’s best for me? Talking therapy can be daunting. If you don’t feel comfortable, it’s possible talking therapy isn’t right for you at this time. If that’s the case, ask your primary care physician about different options that could help instead.

Talking therapy can be challenging and you may feel awkward or nervous at times. But, you’re likely to feel less intimidated as time goes on. During talking therapy, try to: be honest with yourself as you try to understand yourself better talk about what’s on your mind, even if you feel confused by certain feelings or questions You may also get tasks or homework to do between sessions like keeping a diary or trying new ways of behaving. It’s important to do this as you’ll get quicker and better results. Remember, even getting yourself to each session is a huge step forward.

children.text: A risk factor is something that increases your chances of developing a problem, disease or injury. Risk factors relating to your health and wellbeing, activities and surroundings can contribute to a fall. Although hazards within the home often contribute to a fall, more often than not falls are caused by personal risk factors.

Our muscles gradually get weaker as we get older, affecting our strength and balance and making it more difficult to undertake daily activities. As well as normal changes caused by ageing, there are a number of reasons why our muscles get weaker, including: lack of physical activity and exercise conditions like arthritis and polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR)

A number of things can cause poor balance, including: weak muscles health conditions – like stroke and Parkinson’s disease the side effects of some medications Dizziness can also affect balance. Find out how to improve your balance and muscle strength

There are a number of reasons why someone might be dizzy or lightheaded. It’s not normally a sign of anything serious, but should be checked out by a doctor. Understanding why you become dizzy is important to countering the risk. Some of the most common causes include: postural hypotension (orthostatic hypotension) – a drop in blood pressure when getting up from lying or sitting. This can be caused by dehydration, ageing circulation, medical conditions such as Parkinson’s disease and heart conditions and some medications used to treat high blood pressure inner ear problems – like labyrinthitis or benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) problems with your heart rate or rhythm dehydration

If you’re prone to black outs, fainting or losing consciousness, you’re at a high risk of having a fall. Loss of consciousness can be caused by a number of things, including problems with your heart rate and rhythm caused by conditions like: bradycardia (slow heart rate) tachycardia (rapid heart rate) atrial fibrillation (irregular heart rate) Always speak to your primary care physician if you’ve experienced a black out, loss of consciousness or have found yourself on the floor and don’t know why or how. Many of these conditions can be treated successfully.

Problems with our feet – like corns, calluses, bunions, ingrown or thick nails and ulcerations – and footwear that is poorly fitted and inappropriate for the occasion, can also increase a person’s risk of falling. Foot problems can also make it more difficult to exercise and keep active, which is especially important if you’re already unsteady on your feet because of weak muscles or poor balance. Numbness in the feet, sometimes linked to diabetes, can leave you unable to fully sense where your foot is on the floor, leading to an increased risk of a fall. Learn more about looking after your feet

As we get older, problems with memory loss, confusion, difficulties with thinking and problem solving, can become more common. This can affect your ability to judge risky situations, take precautions when moving around your home and recognise hazards, leading to an increased risk of falls.

Problems with your vision and hearing can make it more difficult to move around safely. Eye problems can make it difficult to anticipate and spot slip or trip hazards in your home. As we get older, changes to our depth perception and ability to adjust to changes in lighting can also contribute to the risk of falls. If you wear bifocal or varifocal lenses in your glasses, you might sometimes find it difficult going down steps, stairs and kerbs. Cataracts, glaucoma and vision-related problems linked to stroke or dementia can also increase your risk of falling. Learn more about looking after your vision and hearing

Drinking too much alcohol, especially with some medications, can make you unsteady on your feet and slow your reactions. As we get older, our bodies find it more difficult to process alcohol and we can become more sensitive to its effects, causing an increased risk of falls. Learn more about how much alcohol you should be drinking

If you have a bladder or bowel condition that causes you to rush to the toilet, or visit more often during the day or night, you could be at an increased risk of falling. This is especially the case if you’re already unsteady on your feet or feel dizzy when getting up from sitting or lying down. Continence problems, and the symptoms of bladder irritability, can often be improved with the correct treatment.

A fall might be the first sign of a new or worsening health condition. New, and often temporary, health conditions that can cause falls include: constipation infection — including a bladder, urinary tract or chest infection dehydration sudden confusion (sometimes called delirium) For this reason, you should always speak to your primary care physician practice, or other health professional – such as a physiotherapist or occupational therapist – if you’ve had a fall.

The side effects of some medicines – such as dizziness, lightheadedness, unsteadiness, drowsiness, blurred or double vision and difficulty thinking clearly, and taking more than 4 medicines at the same time, can increase your chance of falling. Medications that most commonly cause these symptoms include: psychotropics (tablets to treat low mood) blood pressure lowering medications sleeping tablets and sedatives anticonvulsants (medication for epilepsy) Side effects can vary from person to person depending on their age, weight, gender, ethnicity and general health, so it’s important that you know and understand how your medication affects you to prevent falls occurring. Learn more about managing your medication

Falls are usually caused by an interaction of a number of risk factors. The more risk factors you have, the greater your risk of falling. Falls prevention is about recognising, and where possible, taking action to reduce the risk. If you experience any, or a combination, of the following you could be at an increased risk: weak muscles, especially in the legs poor balance, causing unsteadiness on your feet dizziness or lightheadedness black outs, fainting or loss of consciousness foot problems – including pain and deformities memory loss, confusion or difficulties with thinking or problem solving vision and hearing problems taking medication that makes you dizzy or drowsy drinking too much alcohol, especially with medication some bladder or bowel conditions

children.text: Anyone can have a trip or fall. As we age, fear of falling can become a serious concern. Some people worry about what might happen to them if they fall, even if they’ve not had a fall before. A fall can leave you feeling shaken up and more cautious. You might stop doing things and lose confidence in your abilities. This is a common reaction and very understandable. However, if you find yourself constantly worrying about falling it can prevent you from having an active and fulfilling life.

Having anxiety about falling is a very common problem – we all have worries and fears. Anxiety can make you feel like you don’t have any control in how you feel and that nothing can be done to change your situation. This can leave you feeling low in mood, frustrated and lonely. You may be embarrassed about having these worries or fear losing your independence if you tell someone your concerns. Many people carry on living with anxiety when they don’t have to. It’s not a sign of weakness or something to be ashamed about.

We all feel anxious at times in our lives, anxiety is our body’s normal reaction to a real or imagined threat or danger. It can develop after any stressful life event such as having a fall. A mild level of anxiety is very common and can often be seen as a normal part of life. However, some people have very strong and constant anxiety and panicky feelings about falling. If this is affecting your life, it has become a problem. Anxiety can affect how you think, what you do and how you feel. It can also be felt in the body, causing symptoms like: rapid, pounding heartbeat headaches chest, shoulder or neck pain feeling dizzy or lightheaded shortness of breath shaky legs nausea loss of appetite butterflies in stomach tightness in muscles These sensations are nature’s way of protecting you from danger. They can be unpleasant, but aren’t harmful, and will go away when your anxiety reduces and you feel calmer. If you have any of these symptoms, speak to your primary care physician who will check your physical health to rule out any health problems. If there are no problems then it’s likely to be anxiety. Find out more about symptoms of anxiety

If you have anxiety about falling, you might: feel irritable and on edge have frequent worrying thoughts and a constant fear of falling. Anxiety can sometimes lead you to overestimate the risk of falling always think the worst will happen focus on just the negative rather than having a positive mental attitude; for example, ‘I can’t walk far because I will fall’ rather than ‘I will try to walk as far as I can and I am going to do the best I can’ Negative thoughts can make things seem worse. Learning to challenge these with thoughts that are more balanced can help reduce any worries. It just takes practice.

The more worried about falling you become, the less likely you are to keep active. Anxiety can make you: act in ways that help you feel safer – such as holding onto things because you think you will fall, or not going out avoid or stop doing things, which can make life difficult, less enjoyable and can lead to low mood and depression You can lose a lot of confidence by avoiding walking. This will affect how you feel about yourself and keep fears going. A cycle of anxiety can develop which keeps fears about falling going. Worrying thoughts can affect how you feel and what you do. Dealing with anxiety can help to improve your mobility, confidence and quality of life. Find out how to deal with anxiety about falling

symptoms_seed.name: Relaxation techniques to help prevent falls

children.text: You should try to set aside 30 minutes, 2 or 3 times each day to practice these techniques. The more you practice, the better you will get and the more effective they will be. It’s important to keep using these techniques, even if you don’t feel better straight away. It will take time and regular practice before you start to feel the benefits.

Before you start relaxing, make sure your mind, body and surroundings are just right. To prepare yourself: find a cool and quiet room where you’ll not be disturbed lie down or sit comfortably with your legs uncrossed put on comfortable clothes and take off your shoes lightly close your eyes, or focus on a spot in front of you clear your thoughts and focus on your breath Don’t worry if you can’t relax immediately. Thoughts might pop into your mind. Don’t focus on them just let them pass through. Make a note of how relaxed you were before, and after, the exercises to see if it’s helped.

Breathing too quickly, and deeply, can make you feel dizzy, faint or even more anxious. Taking slow, regular breaths can help you to control anxious thoughts and feelings, and make you feel calmer. To control your breathing: Place one hand on your chest and the other over your stomach. You want your stomach to move more than your chest as you breathe. Take a slow, regular breath in (through your nose if you can). Watch your hands as you breathe in. The hand on your stomach should move and your chest should not. Breathe out slowly through pursed lips. Repeat this 10 times, twice a day. It might take time to master this technique. Once you have, you won’t need to watch your hands or put them on your stomach.

This exercise involves using an image as a way to focus the mind. Create in your mind an ideal spot to relax. It can be: real or imaginary somewhere you will find restful, calming, safe and happy a place you would want to return to whenever you feel the need to relax Imagine it in as much detail as you can – use your senses to make it as real as possible – and see yourself comfortably enjoying this place. Now close your eyes and take a slow, regular breath in through your nose. Become aware of your breathing. Focus on your relaxation place in all its detail and breathe out through your mouth. Do this exercise for 10 to 20 minutes.

This exercise will teach you to recognise and reduce muscle tension. You can relieve tension in any part of your body just by tensing and relaxing each muscle in turn. Sitting in a comfortable chair: Close your eyes and concentrate on your breathing. Slowly breath in through your nose and out through your mouth. Make a fist, squeezing your hand tightly. Hold this for a few seconds, noticing the tension. Slowly open your fingers and feel the difference – notice the tension leaving. Your hand is much lighter and relaxed. Enjoy this feeling. If you have any physical injuries or conditions that may cause muscle pain, don’t tense the muscle in that area.

Once you’ve mastered some relaxation exercises you can use them whenever, and wherever, you need to throughout the day. To do this you can use a ‘cue’, something that’ll catch your eye and remind you to: drop your shoulders check your breathing relax the muscles in your body An example of a ‘cue’ could be a small coloured dot on your watch, or a room in your home, which will act as your reminder.

Don’t rush to get up after relaxation exercises. Sit with your eyes closed for a few minutes to avoid the possibility of feeling dizzy. Open your eyes and make sure you feel all right before standing up.

children.text: Age is no barrier to exercise. At any age, you can see improvement in your strength, balance, stamina, flexibility and more importantly the mental health benefits of exercise should never be underestimated.

To start with, try each exercise 2 or 3 times and slowly increase the repetitions as you build strength and confidence. For example, in a couple of days you might repeat each exercise 5 times, working up to 10 repetitions in a couple of week’s time. After this time you’ll notice the difference, you’ll see your balance and strength improving, and you feel ready to join a group or class to build on these exercises.
These exercises will help to improve your strength and balance, and build your confidence if you’ve weak muscles or poor balance.

When using a chair or kitchen counter for support, you could start by either: holding on quite firmly touching the chair or table with a finger If you’re feeling particularly confident, hold your hand just above, but have a chair nearby just in case.

Easy marching is a good way to warm up, and keep your circulation flowing, before any exercise. To easy march: Place your feet hip-width apart, relax your body and keep your shoulders down. Start to walk on the spot. As you walk, make sure you put the ball of your foot down first through to the heel. If you feel confident, take your hand off the chair. As you warm up, you may feel that you want to raise your knees a little bit higher for a more purposeful march.

Trunk movements help to improve the flexibility of your spine. To do these movements: Place your feet hip-width apart, and keep your shoulders nice and relaxed. Gently fold your arms in front of you and grow tall. Slowly look over one of your shoulders, making sure your hips stay pointing forward. Repeat this up to 10 times.

Knee strengthening exercises will help you to maintain strength in the muscle at the front of your leg. To strengthen the knee: Sit firmly in the back of a chair, keep your shoulders down and maintain good posture. With or without an ankle weight, slowly extend your leg in front of you. Repeat up to 10 times on each leg.

Hip-strengthening exercises can help to build good leg muscle strength, which will help you get out of the car, or bath, more easily. To strengthen your hip: Place your feet hip-width apart and hold on for support. With or without an ankle weight, slowly take the leg out to the side. Keep looking forward and keep a good posture. Hold it for a count of 4 or 5 seconds.

Calf or heel raises help to build strength in your ankles. Strong ankles are important as they’re first thing that keeps us upright. To do a calf or heel raise: Slowly rise up onto the balls of your feet, with your weight on the big toe and the second toe. Hold for a count of 4 or 5 seconds. Return to standing in a controlled manner, and try not to rock.

Toe raises can help to strengthen the muscles at the front of our feet, which are often weak. These muscles are important as they help to lift our feet over obstacles. To do a toe raise: Hold on to a chair or kitchen counter for support, and stand tall with good posture. Slowly bring your toes up towards your nose. You may not have quite this level of flexibility, but try to raise them as far as you can. Each time you do this, keep your stomach muscles tight and your bottom in. It’s normal to wobble as you practice toe raises.

Moving from sitting to standing is a core exercise that’ll help to improve your strength and balance. You can do this anywhere in your home, but make sure you’ve got a solid chair. There are 3 handholds, you could either: push firmly on the arms of the chair have a light fingertip touch fold your arms and let your legs do all the work, if you’re more confident To sit to stand: Sit forward from the back of the chair to work the back muscles. Make sure you’ve got good posture and that your toes are back under your knees. Slowly stand up, moving your feet a little bit to get the blood flowing again. Slowly sit back again with control. Repeat up to 10 times.
These exercises will help to improve your confidence, muscle strength and balance.

It’s important to maintain flexibility at the ankles, so you can cope with uneven pavements. To move the ankles: Sit at the back of a chair with your back supported and make sure you’re sitting tall. Lift your leg and slowly pull your toes towards your knee. Slowly push your toes away from you and, in a slow and controlled manner, move your toes forward and back to increase the range of motion. Repeat this up to 10 times on each leg.

Knee strengthening exercises will help you to maintain strength in the muscle at the back of your leg. This exercise can be done with or without ankle weights. Hold on to a chair or counter to make sure your balance is good. To strengthen the knee: Stand up tall and pull your leg backwards a touch so that one knee is behind the other but the toe remains on the floor. Slowly lift the heel towards the ceiling. Hold for a slow count of 4.

Knee bends work the muscles at the front of your thigh. Hold on to a chair or counter for support. To do a knee bend: Place your feet hip-width apart, stand up tall and make sure your posture is good. Bend both knees, making sure that they don’t go too far forward and you don’t bend too low. Try to keep looking forward as you do this. Hold for a slow count of 4 or 5, and then rise up again. Repeat up to 10 times.

An effective way to improve balance is to reduce the base of support (the amount of space that your feet take up on the floor). When practising heel-toe standing, make sure that you hold on to a chair or counter to start with. If you can, try to reduce your handhold so that the hand is just above the chair. To do heel-toe standing: Grow tall, and bring one foot in front of the other, touching heel to toe. Transfer your weight so that it’s equal on both feet. Hold for a slow count of 5. Repeat up to 10 times.

Heel-toe walking builds on heel-toe standing by including a movement forward. When practising heel-toe walking, make sure that you hold on to a chair or counter to start with. To do heel-toe standing: Stand up tall and keep looking forward Slowly move one foot in front of the other so that the heel touches the toe. Make sure you’ve got your weight evenly distributed before you start the next step. If you can, take your hand off the chair, but keep it nearby for support. Progress to doing about 10 of these steps.

Sideways walking is another important balance exercise. To do a sideways walk: Place your feet hip-width apart, stand up tall and hold on to something firm. Take one foot out to the side and put the toe down before the heel. Try to keep looking forward. As you bring the other leg to join it, keep a gap between the legs. Depending on the amount of space you’ve got, keep moving to the left and then right until you’ve done about 10 steps. If you can, reduce the handhold over time. If you can, reduce the handhold over time.
These exercises will help to improve your strength and balance further if your balance and muscle strength is already quite good.

Toe walking is another important balance exercise. To toe walk: Start by growing tall and make sure you’ve got something to hold on to. Pull your tummy muscles in and move slowly up on to your toes. When you’re steady, take small, controlled steps on your toes. Try to keep the weight on your big toe and second toe. Look forward as you step. Bring your heels down, turn towards your support then turn around and go in the opposite direction. Aim to do 10 steps in both directions.

This balance exercise is a bit more difficult. Make sure that you’ve got a good solid support to hold on to. To heel walk: Standing tall, pull your toes up towards your nose, keeping your tummy tight and your bottom in. Take small, controlled steps on your heels, looking forward as you step. This can be difficult but try as hard as you can to raise the toes up and keep them up during the walking. Turn towards your support, then turn around and go in the opposite direction. Aim to do 10 steps in each direction, reducing your handhold over time.
Before attempting any of these exercises, it’s important to pick the level that most suits you.

To find out which level to start on, try standing on one leg for 30 seconds while holding on to a chair or table for support. When you’re ready, try to let go: if you don’t feel confident enough to let go, or wobble or have to put a foot down quickly if you do, you should start on level 1 if you have to occasionally hold on or put a foot down, but only occasionally, you can start on level 2 if can manage the full 30 seconds without holding on or putting your foot down, you can start on level 3
You will need support when doing these exercises so find something in your house that’s safe and secure for you to hold on to. Your kitchen counter or a solid chair are good.

symptoms_seed.name: Prevent falls by looking after your vision and hearing

children.text: You might notice your vision changing in the following ways: blurred vision or reduction in ability to see detail of objects (loss of visual acuity) reduced visual field, which is a reduction in what you can see when the eye is looking forward, and includes your peripheral vision less accuracy when you’re judging distances and depth – such as misjudging the height of a step or stairs reduction in your ability to see well in low contrast situations – such as distinguishing similar coloured fixtures and furnishing your eyes taking longer to adjust to changes in the lighting levels – such as when moving from a darkly lit to a brightly lit room Don’t assume that if you can still read the newspaper or watch television that your eyesight is fine. This is not necessarily true. Changes can occur gradually over time, which you may not notice until there’s a significant deterioration.

have your eyes checked regularlyif you need glasses, look after them and have your prescription checked regularlymaintain good lighting throughout your homespeak to your primary care physician if you notice a change in your hearing

You can look after the health of your eyes, and help to prevent eye conditions from occurring, by: quitting smoking keeping active and doing regular exercise eating a balanced diet and limiting how much alcohol you drink protecting your eyes from the sun having regular eye checks If you need to take medication for eye health, make sure you take as prescribed and don’t stop without talking to your primary care physician or optometrist.

It’s very important to have your eyes checked, and your glasses prescription reviewed, regularly. Free eye examinations are available: once every 2 years if you’re between 16 and 59 years old once a year if you’re under 16, or aged 60 or over You’re also eligible for a free eye examination every year if you have: ocular hypertension or diabetes glaucoma, or you’re aged 40 or over and your mother, father, brother, sister, son or daughter has glaucoma This is general guidance and your optometrist may recommend that you attend more frequently.
NHS eye tests are free to all the region residents in the region.

Glasses fitted with bifocal or varifocal lenses can make things appear closer than they really are if you’re looking through the wrong part of the lens. This can cause you to trip or lose your balance – particularly on stairs or going up or down kerbs or steps. Bifocal lenses correct near and distance vision, but provide no correction in-between, whereas varifocal lenses correct near, distance and in-between vision. These types of lenses are prescribed for both near and farsighted people. If you’ve had problems with bifocals or varifocals, or are considering using them, ask your optician for advice. Remember to clean your glasses regularly, and to put them on if you get up in the night. If you receive certain benefits or are on a low income, you may also be entitled to help with the cost of new glasses.

Dementia can affect the way we perceive and process information from our eyes. For example, height and depth can become difficult to judge, making stairs and stepping up kerbs and steps hazardous and causing difficulties when sitting on a chair or bed. As dementia can also affect communication, sight loss can remain hidden if a person is unable to talk about their eye problems. For more about dementia and sight loss, read the RNIB’s advice on sight loss and dementia

To make the most of the useful vision you have as you become older, it’s important to maintain well, even, controllable lighting levels throughout your home to reduce the risk of falling. Learn more about lighting and identifying hazards

Problems with hearing can affect the balance centre in your inner ear, and your awareness of hazards in your environment, making tripping and falling more likely. If you’ve noticed a change in your hearing, speak to your primary care physician as soon as possible. If you suffer from hearing loss, hearing aids are available free on the NHS and can help restore some, if not all, of your hearing. Where to get your hearing tested

Think about how you currently look after your vision and hearing: what positive things do you already do to look after your vision and hearing? what changes can you make that might help? how will you make these changes? who do you need to talk to?

Having your eyes checked regularly can help to detect: age-related changes eye conditions such as cataracts, glaucoma and macular degeneration During your eye examination, you should let the optometrist know if you’ve: ever had a fall any family history of eye conditions like glaucoma
If you’re attending hospital for diabetic retinopathy screening, it’s important to continue to attend your routine eye checks during this time.

RNIB the region provides information and advice to people living with sight loss. If you need to speak to someone, phone their helpline on 0303 123 9999 (Monday to Friday 8.45 AM to 5.30 PM). The Royal National Institute for Deaf People (RNID) provides information and support to people who are deaf or have hearing problems. If you need to speak to someone, phone their helpline on 0808 808 0123 (Monday to Friday 9.00 AM to 5.00 PM) or text phone 0808 808 9000.

symptoms_seed.name: Moving around safely to help prevent falls

children.text: Some of the changes you might notice include: loss of strength and power in leg muscles, which can cause difficulties in carrying out everyday tasks – like getting out of bed, rising from a seat, going up or down stairs or getting dressed shuffling when you’re walking or turning, and difficulties cleaning your feet stiffness and loss of movement at the hips and ankles loss of strength in the upper body and back, which can make you lean forward when you stand and walk tiredness when walking any distance As well as normal ageing, these changes can be a result of: health conditions – like arthritis and Parkinson’s disease new or old injuries lack of physical activity the side effects of some medicines, although this is less common
If you find that you’re getting up to the toilet more frequently in the night, ask your primary care physician for advice.
If you’re having difficulty moving around you might also consider:
If you’re unsteady on your feet and need to get up during the night, planning ahead will help you to move around safely.

make sure that you put a bedside lamp onput on your slippers and glasses, if you wear themsit for a moment on the side of the bed and move your legs in a slow marching action before standing up slowly

Think about how you currently move around inside, and outside, your home: what positive things do you already do to move around safely? what changes can you make that might help? how will you make these changes? who do you need to talk to?

Walk tall, let your arms swing naturally at your sides and look straight ahead. If you can, try to lift your feet and take equal length steps. If you need to look down, do this with your eyes and not your head. Always take your time when getting up from a chair or your bed because your blood pressure can drop when you stand up and your body may take time to adjust. If you feel dizzy when you get up, try moving your legs in a slow marching action before standing up. If feeling dizzy is a problem for you, ask your primary care physician for advice.

symptoms_seed.name: Keeping active to help prevent falls

children.text: be active every day – sit less, move more150 minutes of physical activity each weekmuscle-strengthening and balance exercises twice a week

Older people should aim to be active every day and, if possible, keep to a minimum the amount of time spent sitting for long periods. Keeping active doesn’t necessarily mean going to the gym or doing sports – walking, dancing, active housework, washing the car and gardening are also good ways to keep active. If you don’t usually exercise, any physical activity you can do is better than none at all. For example, when watching television consider: getting up and moving around between programmes or during the adverts taking regular walk breaks around the house, garden or street

Over the course of a week, the time you spend being physically active should add up to 150 minutes (2.5 hours). This can be made up of: short spells of moderate intensity activity – such as 10 minutes of activity, 3 times a day, 5 days a week longer spells of moderate intensity activity – such as 30 minutes of activity, 5 days a week (activities lasting for 10 minutes or more are of more benefit) A moderate intensity activity is one that makes you: feel warmer breathe more heavily, but you should still be able to carry out a conversation If you’re not used to being active, you may find that it won’t take very much activity to reach moderate intensity. If you’re already active, either through daily walking, an active job or engaging in regular exercise, you may still benefit from increasing your physical activity to improve aspects of your fitness.

To reduce your risk of falls, you can also do specific exercises to improve your muscle-strength. Stronger muscles can: improve your balance take some of the strain off painful joints improve your reactions make daily activities – such standing up from your chair, climbing stairs and getting down to the floor – less of an effort As well as doing specific strengthening exercises, you can build up your leg strength by: walking going up and down stairs practising standing up from a chair (if you’re able) If you’ve done an exercise that helps to improve your strength, your muscles will feel warm.

Balance exercise can help you to feel steadier on your feet by challenging your balance. You should feel slightly unsteady when doing these types of exercise as they force your body to get used to working to maintain your balance. You should aim to do balance exercises at least twice a week. Tai Chi is a great activity to maintain and improve your balance. If you’re unsteady on your feet, the Tai Chi instructor may be able to adapt some of the movements to suit you.

You need to do falls prevention exercises regularly for them to be effective. If you regularly do falls prevention exercises given to you by an exercise professional, physiotherapist, occupational therapist or falls specialist nurse keep doing them, unless you are injured or your health has changed.

If you’re new to physical activity and exercise, or haven’t done a lot in a while: start slowly and build up gradually over time always stay within your comfort levels don’t exercise on days you feel unwell always stop exercising immediately if you experience chest pain or feel faint. Contact your doctor for advice To get started: Create an exercise plan – having a routine is a great way to keep you motivated and on target. Use this plan to record what physical activities and strength and balance exercises you’ll do each week and how often. Find supervised groups or classes in your area – exercise classes designed for older people are of particular benefit as they can improve balance and strength. Exercising with others in a class can be fun as well as being good for your health. It can also help to keep you motivated. Join your local gym or sports club – this will give you access to specialised equipment, classes and training from qualified instructors. Most councils offer a discount on gym memberships for people aged 60 or over.

When planning what physical activity and exercise to do, remember that you don’t need to do your strength and balance exercises every day, but you should try to be physically active every day. Plan your physical activity and exercise routine with a friend or partner as this can help you to stay motivated and remove any anxiety or nervousness when doing new activities.

If you have certain medical conditions – such as a heart or lung condition or other condition that makes exercise difficult – there may be some exercises or activities that aren’t suitable for you. If you need help or advice about the best activities for you, speak to your primary care physician, a physiotherapist or qualified fitness instructor.

Think about how you currently keep active and exercise: what positive things do you already do to keep physically active? what changes can you make that might help? how will you make these changes? who do you need to talk to?
Age the region provide more information about healthy living for older people, including ways to stay active. The heart health organization also offer tips and advice for staying active.
