symptoms_seed.name: Prevent falls by identifying hazards at home

children.text: Many falls could be prevented by making a few small changes in your home. These changes may also make it easier getting around your home and carrying out daily activities. It can be helpful to have someone else, such as a friend, relative or neighbour to have a look with you to see if there is anything which could be made safer.
remove or avoid trip and slip hazardsimprove lightingstore frequently used items within easier reachchange or adapt furniture and furnishings to give more support

Think about how you currently keep your home safe: what positive things do you already do identify, and remove, hazards? what changes can you make that might help? how will you make these changes? who do you need to talk to?

An occupational therapist can help you to stay active and safe by: checking how you manage your daily activities arranging for you to get equipment – such as rails or walking aids – to make your life easier helping you find better ways to carry out everyday tasks around the home If you would like further advice, or are having difficulties with everyday tasks, you can ask to be referred to an occupational therapist by contacting your local social work department, or health centre. If you have Parkinson’s disease, and are at risk of falling, Parkinson’s the region have information on occupational therapy and Parkinson’s explaining how occupational therapy can help.

Care and Repair the region provides advice and assistance to enable people aged 60 or over, or who have a disability, to repair, improve or adapt their homes. Home safety is not just important for falls, it can also help to prevent domestic fires for which older people are at most risk. The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service offer free home fire safety visits to help you spot possible fire hazards and fit smoke alarms free of charge if you need them. To arrange a visit for you, or someone you know, phone 0800 0731 {{LOCAL_EMERGENCY_NUMBER}} or text ‘FIRE’ to 80800.

symptoms_seed.name: Prevent falls by doing a home safety check

children.text: To make things safer you could: improve the lighting, ideally having a light switch at both the top and the bottom of the stairs install a handrail, or better still, a handrail on each side clear any items stored on the stairs if you use a walking aid and need to use 2 handrails on the stairs, keep a walking aid at the top and bottom walk on the widest part of the stair, especially if the stair is curved be aware of patterned carpets on stairs as patterns can play tricks on your eyes and cause you to lose balance if you have to carry items while walking up or down stairs, hold the item in one hand and use the handrail with the other be sure you can see where your feet are stepping when you’re carrying something

To make things safer you could: organise your room so you have easy access to curtains, plug sockets and cupboards choose a chair that’s the best height for you to get up from safely – a soft cushion in your chair can make it harder for you to get up safely If you have alarm pull cords, make sure they reach the floor so that you can use them if you fall.

To make things safer you could: choose a bed that is the best height for you to get in and out of safely organise you room so you have easy access to your clothes sit down to get dressed if you’re unsteady on your feet, or get dizzy – especially if you have difficulty with lower garments

To make things safer you could: use a non-slip mat or stickers, if your bath is slippery make sure hand rails anywhere in the bathroom are attached to the wall securely mop up water spills use properly placed hand rails, if you have difficulty getting on and off the toilet, or in and out of the bath use a perch stool if you’re struggling to stand and wash at the sink talk to an occupational therapist or physiotherapist about changing your walking frame if it doesn’t fit in your bathroom – the door can also be changed to make space If you get dizzy or lightheaded, be aware that hot showers and baths can make the symptoms worse.

To make things safer you could: arrange your kitchen so that items that are used regularly are within easier reach keep the kettle near to the sink with cups and tea or coffee beside to save moving around the kitchen too much use a kitchen trolley or, if you have a walking frame, a caddy, to help transport items

Go from room to room and decide what changes you can do yourself and what changes you need extra help with. If you need help to check each room, ask a friend, relative or neighbour to have a look with you.

Occupational therapists work with people of all ages to help them overcome the effects of disability caused by physical or psychological illness, ageing or accident. They can support you to make changes in your home to improve your safety and quality of life. To find out about occupational therapist services from your local authority, contact your local social work department.

symptoms_seed.name: What to do if you fall

children.text: If you’re not hurt and feel well enough, you could try to get up from the floor. The best way will differ from person to person, but as a guide, you can: Roll onto your side. Push yourself up to a side sitting position. Slowly get onto your hands and knees. Crawl towards a sturdy piece of furniture that can support you to get up – such as a solid chair or sofa. Kneel side-on to the chair or sofa with your strongest leg next to it, then slide the foot of your strongest leg forward so that it’s flat on the floor. Your other knee should remain on the floor. Put both hands on the chair or sofa. Raise and turn your body, pushing through your hands and foot until your bottom is safely on the chair or sofa. Sit for a few minutes before you try to do anything else and check again for injuries. If you have weak muscles, or painful and stiff joints in your legs, you may not be able to follow these instructions. In this case, you can consider getting a community alarm so you know that help will always be available. Find out more about telecare services using the Telecare Self-check tool To improve your confidence and technique, it’s a good idea to practice getting up from a fall in different rooms of your house and using different types of sturdy furniture for support. For your safety, ask a friend or relative to be with you when you practice.

After calling for help, it’s important to keep warm as you may be at risk of developing hypothermia. To keep warm: Move onto a carpet, rug or other soft surface. Hard surfaces like tiles and stone floors are often colder and take longer to warm up. If you have to empty your bladder while you’re on the floor, move away from the wet area. Reach for a nearby duvet cover, blanket or clothing that you can use to cover yourself. Move away from areas where there’s a draft. Keep your body moving. If you’re with someone, ask them to put the heating on or make you a hot drink.

You should also attempt to keep your body moving as best you can. Lying in one position for too long can make you stiff, sore and damage the skin. Moving your body, even gently, will keep you warm, focused and calm until help arrives. If you can, try to rock from side to side. If it hurts to move, stop.
If you’re on the floor for a long time, you could become dehydrated. If you have a glass or bottle of water within reach, you can take small sips from it.

Regardless of whether this is your first fall, or you fall regularly, it’s important to tell your primary care physician practice, or other health professional – such as a physiotherapist or occupational therapist. Many underlying causes of falls can be treated or corrected. Learn more about when and where to get help

Think about what you might do if you had a fall: would you know how to get up from the floor, or summon help? do you currently have a falls plan? what changes can you make that might help? how will you make these changes? who do you need to talk to?

The first thing you need to do after a fall is work out if you’re hurt. Take a few minutes to check your body for any pain or injuries, then: if you’re not hurt, try to get up from the floor if you’re hurt or unable to get off the floor, call for help and keep warm and moving as best you can while you wait

You should call for help if you’re hurt as attempting to get up could make your injury worse. You may also need to call for help if you’re unable to get up yourself. To call for help: use a community alarm, if you have one use a phone to call a relative, friend or neighbour; if you’re injured, phone {{LOCAL_EMERGENCY_NUMBER}} and ask for an ambulance; if you’re not sure, phone {{LOCAL_EMERGENCY_NUMBER}} ask your smart speaker, if you have one, to call someone who can help you try shouting, or banging on a wall, to try to attract your neighbour’s attention Having a community alarm, or mobile phone, on you at all times will help you to call for help when you need it. Your mobile phone needs to be charged and switched on all the time. A number to call in an emergency can be programmed into the phone. Ensuring that a family member or neighbour has a spare key will allow people to get to you quickly. You can also consider leaving a spare key in a police-approved key safe. This is a secure box with a combination lock that you can keep outside your home. This can be accessed by anyone that you have shared the combination code with.
If you’ve hurt yourself during a fall, you can find treatment advice for muscle, bone and joint injuries.
It can take a few minutes to feel pain from injuries. If someone else falls it’s important to reassure them, and assess the situation together, before you act.

children.text: If you decide that using a phone is the safest, and most effective, way to call for help, you should consider buying a mobile phone, even if it’s just for emergencies. If you buy a mobile, remember to: keep it charged and topped up with funds if it’s a pay-as-you-go phone keep it on you at all times share your number with a relative or neighbour and tell them that the number is for emergencies – that way, if you run out of battery or lose signal before you have a chance to talk, they’ll know that you need help You can also phone the emergency services for free even if you’ve no credit.

An alarm is something that raises attention that you’ve had a fall. This could be a community (personal) alarm, where you keep a transmitter on you and another person has a receiver. That person could be a relative, friend, neighbour or monitoring service. If you decide to get an alarm, it’s important that you understand the costs involved as some companies may charge you each month for setting up and monitoring your alarm. Learn more about community alarms
Once you have your plan ready, it’s a good idea to share this with your family and friends and let them know what to expect and what to do in the event of a fall.

Telecare is the use of discreet equipment that can help tell if there is an emergency or if you’re having difficulties in your home. Visit the Telecare Self-Check online tool to find the right support for you in your area.

You can call for help many ways. The most important thing is that the person you call expects it and knows what to do. Decide which of the following is the most convenient and effective way for you to call for help: using a phone, autodialer or intercom system using a community (personal) alarm You can also summon help by calling out, or banging on a wall or floor, but this could be difficult if you’re unwell or hurt and it’s too difficult to move. Using a phone, or alarm, is more reliable. You might also consider asking a relative, friend or neighbour to check in regularly, either by phone or by visit.

After deciding how you’ll raise the alarm, you must now think about how they’ll get to you. If you lock your doors when you’re at home, it can be difficult for someone to gain entry. They might have no other option but to force the door. You might consider: leaving a spare key with a friend, neighbour or relative you trust that lives nearby leaving a spare key in a key safe – a secure box with a combination lock that you can keep outside your home which can be accessed by anyone that you have shared the combination code with

symptoms_seed.name: When and where to get help if you’ve had a fall

children.text: If you seek advice and support after a fall, or have concerns about falling, it’s most likely that you’ll be offered a ‘home and person’ falls risk screen. The purpose of the screen is to: listen to what you think the problem could be try to work out why you’re falling agree an action plan with you to reduce your risk of falling, and the risk of being harmed if you were to have a fall Find out more about falls risk screening

If you need support following a fall, or help to reduce your risk of falling, your primary care physician practice, community nurse or other health or social care professional, will be able to advise you where to get support in your area. Some health and social care services have a specialist falls prevention service, however, in most parts of the region services that can help prevent falls are provided by: day hospitals falls clinics community care and rehabilitation teams community physiotherapists community occupational therapists In some areas, you’ll be able to contact many of these services yourself, while in others, your primary care physician might have to refer you.

children.text: Telecare (previously known as community alarms) is a service that offers you support through the use of technology and a way to get help if you’re unable to help yourself. The service is available to anyone of any age. It particularly benefits people: at risk of falls with issues moving around who live in vulnerable situations who have serious health conditions with brain conditions like dementia or epilepsy For example, if you fall and cannot get back up, the telecare service can arrange for someone to come and help you. If you have a loved one who has dementia, there are services that can help keep them safe while remaining at home. Telecare services are available 365 days a year, 24 hours a day. The services are provided by local authorities including: NHS services health and social care partnerships housing providers private companies Telecare is a chargeable service and pricing varies across the region. Some local authorities offer means testing. It may already be included in a service offered by local authorities, such as sheltered housing. The telecare service provider will be able to tell you about costs. Further information about assessment of your care needs.
Telecare is usually made up of an alarm base unit and a peripheral device(s) such as an alarm that you wear. Telecare peripherals connect through radio waves.

The alarms and devices are designed to be as discreet as possible and connect to an Alarm Receiving Centre (ARC) through a phone connection. The peripheral devices trigger the phone for help. Once activated, the call handler in the ARC will: try to speak to you through the alarm box’s built-in microphone and speaker without the need to lift a phone confirm and provide assistance required – this could be phoning a neighbour, relative, friend, or the emergency services; in some areas, there’s also a mobile team who can come and help you Your local provider will be able to confirm which peripheral devices are available and which best suit your needs. A pendant alarm is something you would wear on your wrist or hang around your neck. If you fall or need help, you can press a button on the pendant. This will trigger a call to the ARC. A fall detector is something you would wear on your wrist. If you’re unable to press a button, this alarm can detect falls without pressing anything and can activate a call automatically. A bed monitor alarm sits under your mattress and will activate if you leave or fall out of bed. Services can install detectors that will phone the ARC if smoke, gas or CO2 is detected in your home. The detectors will also phone the ARC if temperatures become too high or low in your property. A door monitor is a small sensor that is placed on your door. It’s often used if you’re at risk of wandering out of the house and getting lost. An epilepsy monitor is something you could wear on your wrist or a monitor on your bed that can activate a call in the event of certain types of seizures. There are devices available that can be worn on your wrist, carried on a keychain or put into your shoes. These devices are used for those who may be at risk of getting lost. A silent alarm is a discreet device that is hidden in your property. It looks like a light switch and can be pressed if you’re vulnerable and at risk from others including cold callers or scammers.

If you would like to get telecare installed for yourself or someone you know, you can either contact: your local authority your local social care service to make a referral You can also get advice about telecare from your: primary care physician practice physiotherapist occupational therapist nurse

symptoms_seed.name: Diet and physical activity tips whilst taking weight loss medication

children.text: Including a source of protein at each meal can help you maintain muscle while you lose weight Try eating the protein part of your meal first to help you get enough protein over the course of the day. There are ways to add more protein to your meals. At breakfast time you could try having: scrambled eggs or tofu a high-protein yoghurt with added fruit or a handful of nuts At lunch or dinner you could try: lean red meat, chicken or fish like salmon or tuna with a salad or cooked vegetables tofu, seitan or other meat substitutes soup or stew with added beans and lentils an omelette reduced-fat cottage cheese on crackers or a baked potato If you feel unable to have a meal you could replace it with a substantial, healthy and nutritious snack. If you are not managing to regularly eat 3 times a day, it may be that your dose is too high. Speak to your prescriber for more advice on this. You can also include high protein snacks to boost your intake. Some examples are: high protein yoghurts protein bars hard boiled eggs packaged cooked meat or non-meat alternatives Diabetes the region have lots of meal plans for different people and dietary preferences. They work just as well for people who don’t have diabetes. Read more about protein on the Eatwell Guide

Include a source of fibre at each meal. Good sources of fibre include: vegetables and fruit with the skin left on pulses like beans and lentils Other examples of high fibre foods include wholegrain cereals, bread, rice and pasta. These will help provide a feeling of fullness. This is because foods high in fibre passes through your digestive system more slowly than lower fibre foods. They will also help prevent constipation. Read more about fibre

Try to drink 2 to 3 litres of fluid each day to avoid dehydration. This could include, or be a combination of: water low-fat milk tea and coffee – although be aware that some speciality drinks like lattes and mochas can be high in sugar and fat diluting juice with reduced or no added sugar fruit juices and smoothies – up to 150ml counts towards your 5 a day

If you feel sick you can try: eating slowly and stopping when you’re satisfied eating smaller meals more often avoiding hot, sugary, spicy, fatty, fried or strong-smelling foods drinking more clear fluids like water – drink in small sips, and not too much at once not lying down soon after eating keeping a food diary of foods and mealtimes to help identify when your side effects get worse Read more about vomitting and nausea in adults

If you feel constipated you can try: drinking more fluids – aim for water or clear drinks, in regular small amounts increasing fibre slowly – like oats, fruit, vegetables, beans and wholegrains keeping active – walking or gentle movement can help your bowels work eating smaller meals and avoiding large, heavy or fatty meals not delaying going to the toilet when you feel the urge trying an over-the-counter laxative like macrogol or lactulose if lifestyle changes don’t help keeping a note of your symptoms to see if they change with dose increases Read more about constipation

If you have diarrhoea, you can try: drinking plenty of water temporarily reducing high fibre foods – you can then gradually bring them back in as your symptoms improve If you’ve been taking laxatives, stop taking these until your symptoms improve. Read more about diarrhoea

There are different ways to be active. These include: strength and resistance exercises cardiovascular (cardio) activity Strength and resistance-based activities help to build muscle. They can also improve your bone health. This is important if you are losing weight quickly using weight loss medications. Some examples of strength and resistance-based activities are: using your own body weight, like doing press ups or squats using therabands or resistance bands doing heavy gardening using exercise machines in a gym These types of activities should be done on at least two days a week, but any strengthening activity is better than none. Try to use all your main muscles – your arms, legs, back and tummy. Bands, weights, or body weight exercises like squats and lunges can be used. Work at a level where your muscles feel tired, but stop if it hurts. Remember to breathe normally and have water nearby. Cardio or aerobic activities make you feel like you are breathing faster and deeper. They help improve your overall fitness. Cardio activities can include: brisk walking stair climbing swimming cycling wheeling Aim to be active in these ways on most days. Try to build up to 150 minutes a week, in chunks that suit you. This could be 30 minutes on 5 days, or shorter sessions spread across the week. Read more about physical activity guidelines

Weight loss medicines help you manage your appetite and regulate your food intake, so you may feel full with smaller amounts of food. Because you’re likely to eat less, it is essential what you do eat provides the right balance of nutrients.

Some of the side effects of weight loss medications are: feeling sick (nausea) constipation diarrhoea These side effects are very common when you first start taking the medication or when you go up a dose. You may experience more than one. There are ways you can still eat and drink whilst having these symptoms.

It’s important to be physically active when taking weight loss medications. Some people taking weight loss medication will experience rapid weight loss. This will result in muscle mass loss (sarcopenia). Improving your strength, alongside eating a nourishing diet with enough protein, will minimise muscle mass loss. Regular physical activity can also help reduce side effects caused by the weight loss medications like nausea and constipation. Read more about weight loss medications

ghana_statistics.comparison_note: Ghana has made progress in reducing stunting from 28% in 2008 to 18% in 2022, aligning with sub-Saharan Africa trends.

symptoms_seed.name: Making a plan that works for you

children.text: Change can be hard because life is full of distractions, stress, habits and competing priorities. Setting goals and making a plan can help you: focus on something simple make healthy choices more easily remember why you’re doing this in the first place Having even a rough plan makes it easier to follow through, and adjust when things don’t go as expected.

Goals don’t have to be big. A useful goal is a small, clear action. For example, a goal like “eat better” is too vague. “Cook dinner at home three nights this week” is clear and doable. Clear goals give your brain a simple instruction and they also make it easier to notice your progress.

MAP is a simple tool to help you set goals you can stick to. It helps you think about why the goal matters (Motivation), what small step you’ll take (Action), and cues that will nudge you to take action (Prompts). Here are some examples of goals and how you can use MAP to plan them.

Take a minute to write down your plan for this week. Try to include: goal – one small change I want to try is… motivation – it matters to me because… action – I’ll do it on (day/time) prompt – what will remind me to do it Review it at the end of the week.
Change isn’t always smooth. It helps to ask yourself: what might get in the way? what would help me keep going? Sharing your plan with someone you trust can help you stay motivated.
Here are some examples of common challenges you might have experienced and some suggestions to overcome them.
Once a week, take a few minutes to reflect on: what went well what was difficult what could I do differently next time This isn’t about judging yourself. It’s about learning what works.

Some weeks will feel easier than others. If things don’t go to plan, that’s okay. If you ever feel stuck, ask yourself; what’s one small thing I could try this week that might help? Small steps add up. Each time you plan ahead or try something new, you’re building healthy habits that last.

symptoms_seed.name: How do I maintain my weight loss?

children.text: Take a moment to recognise your achievements. Celebrating small steps can help keep you motivated. Before looking ahead, take a moment to reflect on how far you’ve come. What’s changed for you since you started? This could be what you eat, how active you are, how you feel, or how you’ve learned to manage tricky situations. Try asking yourself: what small or big changes have I made? what improvements do I want to continue? what’s helped me stay motivated? Writing down your answers can help you spot patterns and plan for what comes next. You could write this down in a journal or app. Some people also like to keep a photo log. This can help you stay on track.

Long-term change isn’t always easy. You might feel confident some weeks and struggle others. This is normal. Life is full of events and situations that make it difficult to maintain your weight, like: holidays or nights out celebrations moving jobs a bereavement feeling stressed or low seasonal changes or weather challenges These situations are part of life. What matters is having a plan that helps you respond positively.

One of the most effective ways to support weight maintenance is to plan ahead. This could mean: choosing lower-calorie options when eating out balancing a celebratory meal by planning healthier options the day before and after scheduling time to be active around a busy period preparing meals in advance For meal ideas, find inspiration from recipes from Let’s Get Cooking and Parent Club. Diabetes the region also have some ideas and suggestions for planning meals on a budget. What works will be different for everyone. The key is making a plan you feel confident about and are able to adjust when needed.

Many people find it helpful to continue: setting small weekly goals tracking progress using a journal, app or photos checking in with how they’re feeling, not just what they’re eating revisiting helpful resources you’ve used Find information on apps and websites that can help

symptoms_seed.name: How do I measure my Body Mass Index (BMI)?

children.text: BMI is useful to measure trends across groups of people but it isn’t perfect for individuals. It measures whether a person is carrying too much weight, but not too much fat. But it can offer a starting point for thinking about your health. It doesn’t take into account things like: high muscle mass (like athletes) bone density age sex ethnicity fluid retention loss of a limb
The NHS website for the region provide a calculator to calculate BMI for children and young people. This is designed for those between the ages of 2 and 17.

You can use the NHS website for the region BMI calculator to work out your BMI. It can also show you what a healthy range might look like for someone of your height. You should not use this tool if you, or the person you’re using it for: are under 18 years old are pregnant have been diagnosed with an eating disorder, or think you may have one have a condition that affects your height

If you have a white family background, your BMI will be in one of these categories: under 18.5 – underweight 18.5 to 24.9 – within the healthy range 25 to 29.9 – overweight 30 to 39.9 – obesity 40 or above – severe obesity If you have an Asian, Chinese, Middle Eastern, Black African or African-Caribbean family background you’ll need to use a lower BMI score: 23 to 27.4 – you’re in the overweight range 27.5 or above – you’re in the obese range If you are from one of these family backgrounds, you have a higher chance of developing health problems at a lower BMI. The NHS website for the region BMI calculator includes adjustments for this.

A BMI in the overweight range can increase your risk of certain conditions. These include: type 2 diabetes high blood pressure heart disease Many things contribute to your health. It’s not just about weight. Your diet, physical activity, sleep, stress and environment all have an affect. If you have a higher BMI, it doesn’t mean something is wrong. But it may be worth looking at some of the factors that support your overall wellbeing. Making small changes to your lifestyle can improve your: energy mood longer-term health Losing 5% to 10% of your body weight, and keeping it off, can lead to improvements in your overall health.

BMI isn’t the only way to understand your weight. Waist-to-height ratio is another way to identify excess weight around your tummy. Waist-to-height-ratio is normally used alongside BMI. The waist to height calculator may not be suitable if: you’re an adult with a BMI over 35 the person you’re using it for is under 5 years old you’re pregnant you’ve been diagnosed with an eating disorder, or think you may have one you have a growth disorder or any other condition that affects your height

children.text: Food and drink give us calories (kcal), which are units of energy. On average, adults need around 2000 kcal a day for women and 2500 kcal a day for men to maintain current body weight. This can vary a lot between people so it’s only a broad guide. If you take in more calories than you use, the body stores the extra as fat. To lose weight, aim for 1,400 kcal a day for women and 1,900 kcal a day for men. These numbers are only rough guides. Age, body size, health, and how active you are all play a part. When you cut calories, move more and successfully lose weight the body often adapts in ways that make further weight loss harder. These are the same reasons why keeping the weight off is also difficult: our body may burn fewer calories hunger levels may increase we may feel more tired This is why losing weight can feel tough, even with healthy changes. Your body is built to hold on to energy, to defend against weight loss and the world around you. This makes it easy to eat and drink more than you need. The good news is while you can’t control everything around you, making small, realistic changes can still have a big impact over time. The key is finding what works for you. Read about tips for losing weight safely

You need food to stay healthy and keep going. Sometimes, how you feel about food and how you eat, can get complicated. Things like past experiences, stress or when times are hard can affect how you eat. Some people: find that eating helps them feel better when they’re upset eat to celebrate or reward themselves While this can be normal, some people find this becomes how they deal with emotions or reward themselves. This can lead to putting on weight without them meaning to. If you find that these feelings get overwhelming, speak to your healthcare professional. Read more about mental wellbeing

Reaching and maintaining a healthy weight isn’t just about numbers. It’s about how you feel every day. A healthy weight can help you: sleep better feel more confident feel more energetic It can also help to reduce your risk of serious conditions like: type 2 diabetes heart disease stroke high blood pressure (hypertension) some types of cancer Any steps you take towards losing weight will bring benefits for your health and wellbeing. This can include: moving more sitting less making small changes to what you eat You don’t need drastic changes to feel a difference.

You might be thinking more about your weight if you’ve noticed changes in how you feel or how your body looks. For example: your clothes feel tighter – like trousers or jeans feeling too tight you’ve been less active than usual your eating habits have changed you’ve had a life event, like starting a new job, that’s affected your routine you feel more tired or uncomfortable in your body The most common tool to check whether you’re in a healthy weight range is Body Mass Index (BMI). It uses your height and weight to give you a general idea about whether you’re a healthy weight. BMI isn’t perfect and doesn’t tell the whole story. Things like muscle mass, age and body shape also matter. However, it can be a useful starting point for thinking about your health. Read more about BMI including how to calculate it

children.text: Try to lose weight gradually – about 1 to 2 pounds (0.5 to 1kg) per week is a safe and healthy pace. Quick fixes are hard to sustain, and the results usually don’t last. Any change to move towards a healthy weight or any weight loss is a step in the right direction.

Fad diets often promise rapid weight loss with little evidence. They tend to be restrictive, hard to follow and may lack essential nutrients. Focus on long-term balance, not quick fixes. Read more from the BDA about fad diets

Choose foods like: vegetables and fruits whole grains lean proteins like fish, beans, or poultry sources of healthy fats like olive oil, nuts, and seeds These foods are healthy and help you feel full. Read more about how to eat a healthy, balanced diet
Use smaller plates and check serving sizes. Paying attention to portion size can help reduce overeating without needing to count every calorie.

Some foods can be high in calories, sugar, salt and fat like: ready meals crisps biscuits fast food It’s easy to overeat these, especially when life is busy or stressful. Some drinks, like sugary soft drinks and alcohol, can add a lot of hidden calories without making us feel full. You don’t have to give them up completely. Even small swaps or cutting back a little can make a big difference over time. NHS the region has a snacking swap app called the NHS Food Scanner app. This can help you choose lower calorie snack options.
Avoid eating when doing something else, like working, watching TV, or while on your phone. This can cause you to overeat. Take your time, enjoy your food, and notice when you feel full.

Many pre-packaged foods display nutrition information on the front of the packet. The information is normally displayed using a colour-coded system. The colours show if the product contains high, medium or low levels of fat, sugars and salt. Look for products with more green colour coding than amber and red. They’re usually the healthier choices. Read more about food labelling

Try to be active in a way you enjoy. Activities like walking, swimming, cycling, wheeling and dancing all count. Mixing in some muscle strengthening activities is great too. Some examples of strengthening activities are: lifting weights yoga heavy gardening carrying heavy shopping Read more about keeping active

Poor sleep and high stress can lead to weight gain. Aim for 7 to 9 hours of sleep and find ways to relax, like going for a walk or doing something you enjoy. Find out how other people manage stress and sleep better

Set small, achievable goals. Expect ups and downs and remember, everyone has off days. What matters is getting back on track without feeling guilty. Practice kind self-talk. Instead of saying “I failed,” try saying “I’m learning what works for me” or “that didn’t go as planned, and that’s okay.” Reward yourself for progress in non-food ways, like: a relaxing walk a favourite podcast some quiet time Remember, ups and downs are normal. Each challenge is a chance to figure out what works for you. The goal is progress, not perfection.
Planning ahead is important to help ensure you have the right foods to hand, at the right times. It will also help you to stay motivated and on track. Read more about making a plan that works for you
Speak to a healthcare professional before starting to lose weight if you have an eating disorder. Read more about eating disorders

You don’t have to do it alone. Reaching out to a friend or family member for support can help you to stay motivated. Speaking to a doctor, dietitian, or support group can also help you stay on track and feel more confident. Find where to get support to help you lose weight

ghana_statistics.prevalence: Ghana is experiencing a nutrition transition. Adult overweight prevalence is approximately 25-30%, while obesity affects about 10-15% of adults.
ghana_statistics.affected_population_estimate: Approximately 5-7 million adults are overweight or obese. Rising trends in urban adolescents.
ghana_statistics.geographic_distribution: Higher rates in urban areas (Accra, Kumasi, Sekondi-Takoradi) compared to rural areas.
ghana_statistics.age_distribution: Adults 30-60 most affected. Rising rates among adolescents in urban schools.
ghana_statistics.risk_factors_in_ghana: Sedentary lifestyles, increased consumption of processed foods, urbanization, shift from traditional to Western diets.
ghana_statistics.health_system_response: Limited dedicated weight management programmes. Some private clinics offer diet and exercise counselling. National NCD policy includes obesity prevention.
ghana_statistics.comparison_note: Ghana's obesity rates are lower than South Africa but higher than neighboring Burkina Faso and Mali.
ghana_statistics.source: WHO STEPwise Survey Ghana; Ghana Statistical Service
